cards.title: Per-kg moments and powers were divided by another participant's body mass
cards.short: 52 of 488 recordings shown; 434 cannot be told or only probably
cards.wrong: For 9 of 12 participants, the authors did not use the person's own body mass to turn moments and powers into per-kg values in level walking. For 7 of them the mass used is exactly another participant's listed body mass, and it can change between recordings of the same person.
cards.how: The source gives some recordings in newton-metres as well as per kg. Dividing one by the other gives the mass that was used. Where that was not possible, the mass was estimated from force-plate moments.
cards.where: Decided by José on 23 November 2026, replacing his 2 November decision of no rescaling: fix the 52 recordings shown to carry another mass. Their moments and powers get rescaled to the person's own mass (multiplied by the mass used divided by the own mass). The other 436 recordings, where the mass used cannot be told, stay as published, with a note. Fix not yet run. The 52 are the recordings where rescaling lowers the error in every plausible case: 7 have the mass used worked out exactly and 45 have it estimated from force plates. José confirmed on 23 November 2026 that all 52 are rescaled. Needs: the mass used for each recording (exact for 7, estimated for the rest, both in the audit files) and the person's own mass from the source's participant table. Not checked: any rescaled output.
cards.example: AB10, turn and step 1: the person's own mass is 67.5 kg, but force-plate moments point to about 83 kg being used. Published error against the person's own mass is 22 to 25%. This recording was drawn at random from the 45 shown recordings with a validated walking estimate.

cards.total_line: 52 of 488 recordings (10.7%) are shown to carry another mass; 15 more (3.1%) probably do; 2 are confirmed to use the person's own mass; 419 cannot be told. In level walking, 9 of 12 participants are affected.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings are the source's 488 recordings from 12 participants. In level walking the affected per-kg values are 0.80 to 1.41 times the value for the person's own mass. Sample counts were not part of these checks.

cards.title: The README says moments are in N·m and powers in W, but the data are per kg
cards.short: All 488 recordings; the check covered 5 participants
cards.wrong: The publisher's README lists joint moments in N·m and powers in W. The published values were already divided by body mass, so they are in N·m per kg and W per kg.
cards.how: A moment rebuilt from the force plates in N·m is 64 to 90 times larger than the published ankle moment, which is a body mass. Joint power equals the published moment times joint speed (ratio 0.96 to 1.00).
cards.where: Documented. LocoHub's converters copy the values and label them per kg, and do not divide by mass a second time, so the labels are already right. Nothing was changed in the data.
cards.example: AB01, incline walking 2, left leg: read as N·m, the published ankle moment is 1/64 to 1/90 of the force-plate moment, in all 8 sampled legs (98 to 99% too small).

figures.question: What if we trust the README and read the values as N·m?
figures.alt: One stance of ankle moment: read as N·m, the published curve is far smaller than the force-plate moment.
figures.caption: Before: read as the README says.

figures.question: Do the values match once we read them as per kg?
figures.alt: The same stance read as per-kg values, matching the force-plate moment divided by a body mass.
figures.caption: After: read as LocoHub does.

cards.total_line: All 488 recordings (100%) carry the README's wrong unit text. The check measured 5 participants (25 channel files, 8 legs) and found the same result in all.
cards.denominator_text: The README applies to every recording. The units check itself sampled 5 of 12 participants; the other 7 are covered by the README text only. Sample counts do not apply.

grid.caption: Every recording is covered by the wrong README text (all of them).

cards.title: Forces in body weights use the wrong mass for AB03
cards.wrong: Both converters take the body mass for body-weight forces from a local table that was rewritten from the body models. For AB03 it says 82.18 kg, but the publisher's table and the force plates say about 113.5 kg. The other participants in the table differ by rounding only (below 0.1%).
cards.how: The publisher's mass table and the local table were compared. In the force-plate check, AB03's body mass came out near 114 kg, not 82.
cards.where: Open. The supported correction is to use the publisher's table. No data have been converted with it yet.
cards.example: AB03 forces divided by 82.18 kg instead of 113.5 kg come out 1.38 times too large in body weights.
cards.total_line: 40 of 488 recordings (8.2%) from 1 of 12 participants: every AB03 recording would get forces in body weights that are 38% too large.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). Sample counts do not apply: this is a conversion setting, and no AB03 recording was converted with the corrected table.

cards.title: Horizontal ground force is labelled forward and sideways, but is in lab axes
cards.short: 398 of 488 recordings that the converters export
cards.wrong: The converters write the force plates' horizontal force in lab directions straight into the forward and sideways columns. Lab directions turn with the person, so they are not forward and sideways unless the person walks along one lab axis.
cards.how: The paper says the forces are in the lab frame. The converter code copies them without turning them by the person's facing direction.
cards.where: Open. A correction tool exists that sets the four forward and sideways force columns to empty and keeps the original values under lab-axis names. It has been tested only on made-up data, not on real data, and has not been run.
cards.example: Walking in a straight line can keep one lab axis nearly fixed, so the error can hide there; a turn or a side shuffle shows it at once.
cards.total_line: 398 of 488 recordings (81.6%) have event windows and would be exported with the wrong labels; the other 90 are never exported by either converter.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). Samples were not counted: nothing was converted for this review.

cards.how: The authors' task descriptions were read, and the heading of the pelvis during each window was reviewed; only the 11 forward-walking tasks have a steady heading that matches the direction of travel.
cards.where: Decided: José asked us to choose, and we took the smallest change. Forward and sideways force and pressure point are filled only for the 11 forward-walking tasks, from the measured facing direction. The other 15 tasks keep lab-axis values only. Not yet run.
cards.example: One of the 15, drawn at random: twister. Its horizontal force stays in lab axes.

cards.title: The pressure point's origin is the heel bone, not a point 100 mm forward of the ankle centre
cards.short: 398 of 488 recordings that the converters export
cards.wrong: The converters give the centre of pressure (where the force acts on the foot) in a frame attached to the heel bone, which turns with the foot. The origin is the heel-bone frame origin, not the ankle as a code comment says. LocoHub's data reference now says the frame turns with the foot and its origin is 100 mm forward of the ankle joint centre along the heel-to-toe direction.
cards.how: The calculation was read: the pressure point in the lab is turned into the foot frame using the foot's position and orientation, with no ankle offset.
cards.where: Decided by José on 23 November 2026: the pressure point is given in a frame that turns with the foot, with its origin 100 mm forward of the ankle centre along the foot's heel-to-toe direction. Fix not yet run. Needs: the ankle centre and the foot's orientation. The converters already use the heel bone's position and orientation, and the mass audit located the ankle centre in the heel-bone frame for the recordings it checked. Whether the ankle centre and heel-to-toe direction are available for every recording: not checked.
cards.example: Moving the origin from the heel-bone frame origin to a point 100 mm forward of the ankle centre shifts every forward and up value by a fixed amount in the foot frame. The size of that shift was not measured.
cards.total_line: 398 of 488 recordings (81.6%) have a pressure point in the foot frame; the other 90 are never exported.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). Samples were not counted.

cards.title: The source's knee sign is opposite to LocoHub's
cards.wrong: The authors' plotting code and paper show hip and knee in the extension-positive direction for the segmented data, and the ankle in the dorsiflexion-positive direction. LocoHub's rule needs flexion positive for hip and knee. The knee therefore needs its sign flipped, in angle, speed and moment; hip and ankle stay as they are.
cards.how: The authors' plotting code was read for its sign changes and the paper's description of the plots. The sign detector was then run on 3 participants.
cards.where: Decided: José chose the rule that the named direction is positive, and this recipe follows it. It has not been applied to the data. It was reproduced from the data only for walking, inclines, declines and stairs in 3 participants.
cards.example: AB01, AB06 and AB13 were checked on level, incline, decline and stair walking: the detector gave a sign for 141 of 180 channel checks and none was wrong; for 39 it gave no answer.
cards.total_line: All 488 recordings (100%) need the knee flip. 20 recordings (4.1%) were checked on real data: 141 of 180 channel checks right, 0 wrong, 39 no answer.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). The checks counted 20 recordings and 180 channel checks (hip, knee and ankle angle, moment and power). Samples were not counted.

grid.caption: Recordings that need the knee sign flip (all of them). Only 20 of them were checked on real data.

knock_on.line: The sign is opposite to LocoHub's until the flip is applied.
knock_on.evidence: Author plotting code and paper, plus 19 of 20 knee-angle and 18 of 20 knee-moment channel checks right in the pilot; the rest gave no answer.

knock_on.signal: Hip and ankle angle, speed and moment
knock_on.line: They already have the LocoHub sign.
knock_on.evidence: Pilot: hip angle 20 of 20, ankle angle 20 of 20, ankle moment 20 of 20 and hip moment 17 of 20 checked right; none wrong.

knock_on.line: Power keeps its sign when moment and speed flip together. The pilot could judge ankle power in 17 of 20, hip power in 10 of 20 and knee power in none of 20.

cards.title: Pelvis, thigh and shank angles are not in the source
cards.wrong: The publisher gives joint angles (hip, knee, ankle) but no pelvis, thigh or shank angles. The local files that have them were made by our own earlier processing (a fixed turn order with a quarter-turn offset for the pelvis), which is not the publisher's definition.
cards.how: All 7,038 entries in the publisher's archive were searched and none holds segment angles or segment speeds.
cards.where: Decided by José on 23 November 2026: compute pelvis, thigh and shank angles as the data reference defines them (thigh and shank from straight down, pelvis from forward horizontal, all measured against gravity). Fix not yet run. Needs: the body segments' orientations. The local transform tables are said to allow pelvis tilt to be computed from them; whether every recording has them: not checked. Nothing is invented.
cards.example: Pelvis tilt for AB02's level walking could be computed from the local transform tables. Its sign and zero are now set by the data reference; no source value exists to check it against.
cards.total_line: All 488 recordings (100%) lack publisher segment angles.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). Seven AB02 windows also have oversized transform tables (see the oversized-table card).

knock_on.evidence: The sign-detector pilot measured it from markers on the front and back of the pelvis.

cards.title: The README and the paper describe joint speed differently
cards.wrong: The README says joint speed is a one-step backward difference of the angle. The paper says the angles were filtered and differentiated with a centred difference. Both cannot be right.
cards.how: The README text, the paper's methods and the authors' code were compared.
cards.where: Documented, kept as published. The published speeds are copied unchanged. No recomputation recipe is claimed, and no speed was replaced to match a preferred shape.
cards.example: Which difference was used decides how smooth the speed looks near fast changes, such as heel strike.
cards.total_line: All 488 recordings (100%) carry joint speeds with an unconfirmed recipe.
cards.denominator_text: Recordings in the source (488). Samples were not counted.

knock_on.line: A recomputation would need the right recipe, which is not established.

cards.title: The time export merges all of a file's events into one window
cards.wrong: The time-based converter makes one window per event file, from the earliest start to the latest end of every field in it. Files that hold several conditions (such as sitting and standing, or forward and backward) become one window that includes the time between them. The reference leg is simply the first start.
cards.how: The converter code was read, and its window count was compared with the authors' counts.
cards.where: Open, fix not yet run. The fix is one window per source interval, labelled by its field. Update, 23 November 2026: José decided that LocoHub segments every recording itself and checks against the authors' labelled strides, so event windows are expected to come from our scripts instead; not yet run.

cards.title: A backup segmentation could replace the source's events
cards.wrong: When an event file lacks left and right fields, the phase converter replaces the source events with its own segmentation using fixed force thresholds (600 and 400 N). Any output made that way is not source-defined.
cards.how: The converter code was read, and every sit-to-stand and jump event file was found to have source fields, so the backup should never run.
cards.where: Open, fix not yet run. The fix is to remove the backup so the converter stops instead. Update, 23 November 2026: José decided that LocoHub segments every recording itself and checks against the authors' labelled strides, so event windows are expected to come from our scripts instead; not yet run.

cards.title: The converter wrote stair, curb and step heights nobody measured
cards.wrong: The converter writes a stair height of 0.15 m (the paper says 152 mm), calls the pass number a step number, and writes 0.15 m for curbs and 0.20 m for step-ups. The curb and step-up heights are not in any local source.
cards.how: The converter's task-detail code was compared with the paper's Table 1. The paper's supplementary protocol table is not available locally.
cards.where: Open, fix not yet run. The fix is stair rise 0.152 m citing the paper, a renamed pass number, and no curb or step-up height unless a source gives one.
